summary: Comments by two early network people on the mail protocol proposed in RFC 524. They call it very rich but point out minor and major problems, such as the use of the Telnet Go-Ahead signal by a higher-level protocol and what the default signature should be. They also suggest that senders be able to give mail a priority.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reviews a proposed network mail protocol and lists changes the authors would like to see. Their comments cover message details, how mail relates to FTP, and rerouting.

subtitle: Crocker and Postel's review of the mail protocol proposed in RFC 524.

tldr.problem: The authors considered the proposed mail protocol rich but identified details that could make it difficult to implement or use.
tldr.mechanism: They list comments on signatures, priority, message size, parameter order, FTP, and mail forwarding, including a suggested reply for rerouting a recipient.
tldr.outcome: RFC 539 offers review comments and proposals rather than defining a mail protocol.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 539 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. RFC 555 later responds to comments on RFC 524, including this review.

sections.title: Message Details and Priority
sections.content:
Crocker and Postel say the proposal is very rich, then raise several smaller points. They suggest using the author's sign-on or identification as the default signature, allowing a sender to describe message size, and changing INTERRUPT to URGENT or PRIORITY.

They also suggest optional levels of urgency, while noting that the proposal should explain how a receiving server would use them.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want a message to identify its writer and give readers a sense of its size and urgency. They ask the protocol to make those details clearer.

sections.title: Command Order and Identification
sections.content:
The authors question how an ID command proves identity across hosts and ask how acknowledgments or replies work without a reference serial number. They also want the formal syntax to show the distinction between static and dynamic attributes.

They recommend sending dynamic and optional parameters before static ones, so a receiving host can consider priority and length before accepting or forwarding a message.
sections.plainLanguage: Some details need clearer rules, including how a sender proves identity and how replies refer to earlier mail. Sending important routing details early could help a server decide what to do.

sections.title: FTP and Mail Forwarding
sections.content:
The authors favor a unified access approach but say the proposed mail protocol should use FTP rather than be an FTP subsystem, following the model used for Remote Job Entry. They note that this raises the issue of logging in to send mail.

They also propose rerouting a message before the receiving host accepts it. A reply could name an alternate location for the intended recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want mail to use FTP without being folded into FTP itself. They also want a server to direct the sender elsewhere when a recipient is at another location.
